horoscopes.intro: November 20 in the stars: Find out what’s in store for you today in our daily horoscopes for Friday November 20. Read the daily horoscopes for your Sun sign or rising sign (ascendant) to plan your day.

aries.text: There’s no such thing as TMI for you today, Aries. With the moon in your sign, you’re in your live-out-loud element. Don’t feel bad about being so…overt. Your bold authenticity will actually create a safe space in which others can open up. Own your past, Aries! Those “embarrassing” mishaps birthed golden lessons that you can pass on to others who are struggling with the same issues. With all that wisdom to share, maybe you could record a podcast or do a live event on social media in the name of inspiring others.

taurus.text: You’re in an emo groove today, Taurus, so just go with it. This is one of those moments where you’d benefit from setting aside that diligent work ethic so you can bond with the people in your environment. Power down your laptop and go have lunch with a colleague. You might even get the chance to pass along some of your sage wisdom to someone who is struggling with an issue you’ve overcome. Reach up to mentors, too, especially one who’s been in your corner in the past. Send an email or set up a time to meet. That guidance can save you a ton of time and money.

gemini.text: Lighten up about love today, Gemini. With the moon in your “the more, the merrier” eleventh house, you could turn that table for two into a setting for six or eight. If your friend group has yet to meet your S.O., this could be the perfect evening to make introductions. Single? Sparks might fly with a friend of a friend. That’s a good reason to meet people after work instead of autopiloting home to watch Netflix with your cat. The number one aphrodisiac for you today (and really, every day) is a fierce sense of humor.

cancer.text: Be more purpose-driven in your personal life today, Cancer. People adore you, and there are plenty of friendships you COULD cultivate. But since each one requires an investment of time, reserve your energy for those who fill your cup. Have you been overloading your calendar with “meh” events out of fear of being lonely? Solitude can be a rich and rewarding thing for your sign; it’s when you’re most creative! Review your schedule and clear white space for a few date nights with the muse.

leo.text: Bigger, stronger, faster: Well, why not, Leo? Today’s moon in your expansive ninth house could bring rapid expansion to one of your goals. Take your foot off the brake, but keep your hands on the wheel. You of all people know that progress CAN happen at supersonic speed. People from other parts of the globe could be involved, so get ready to log into WhatsApp and brainstorm away! To accelerate the process, you might have to take a risk. Make sure it’s a calculated leap instead of a hasty gamble.

virgo.text: Got secrets? One of those skeletons is rattling the closet door, begging to be freed. Time for a confessional conversation, Virgo—the truth will liberate your soul. Connect with a trusted ally tonight, either on FaceTime or huddled in a private corner. And if you’re looking for sympathy, not advice, make sure to state that up front. Coworkers may park at your desk for an impromptu “therapy” session. Watch the clock! Those conversations can suck up valuable minutes, making you late for your evening tête-à-tête.

libra.text: People-watching is one of your favorite hobbies, and today, it could evolve into a fascinating dialogue. If someone’s reading a book that changed your life or wearing a piece by your favorite indie-label designer, strike up a conversation. Your journalistic curiosity could unearth fascinating synergies and, potentially, a love connection. In a relationship? Apply the Buddhist concept of “beginner’s mind.” Approach your S.O. as if you’re meeting for the first time. When you drop assumptions and ask questions instead, you might be pleasantly surprised.

scorpio.text: How hard can it possibly be, Scorpio? If you’re stressing over the complexity of a problem, maybe YOU shouldn’t be the one trying to untangle the knot. With today’s moon in your house of helpful people, support could be a text message away. Your time is valuable, and the hours of frustration you save will be worth the expense of calling for backup. Don’t worry about “burdening” anyone. You’ve supported so many, it shouldn’t be too tough to find someone willing to back you up in return.

sagittarius.text: Put a little luxe in your life. Today’s decadent Aries moon gives you a hall pass to be hedonistic. This doesn’t have to be harmful to your health or the planet. Looking for a signature accessory for fall? Find a sustainable jeweler who repurposes gold and gems from antique pieces. This romantic lunation can turn up the heat with a love interest. Slip off for a lunch date, and don’t be surprised if it turns into a spicy nooner. What can you do to lure friends out for some cultural activities this Friday night?

capricorn.text: Bless this mess? Not today! With the Aries moon percolating in your domestic fourth house, tidying up your space could lead to sharper thinking. As you’re wiping down surfaces and deleting junk mail, you may become acutely aware of emotions that you pushed aside. The truth? It’s actually more painful to resist them than it is to finally face them. If you’re not ready to confront the challenging circumstances, open up to a close friend about your confusion. Clarity might be a (teary) conversation away. Deal, then heal.

aquarius.text: The Aquarius social butterfly is bursting out of the cocoon thanks to today’s lunar lift in your communication corner. Since you won’t have much patience for desk work, rejig your schedule so you can handle the people-oriented tasks on your to-do list. A spontaneous lunch date with a coworker could turn into an amazing brainstorming session that leaves you both buzzing with inspiration. With the moon in restless Aries, slip out for fresh-air breaks. Who says you can’t take a walk during that conference call? This flirty energy could make you quite the charmer, and anywhere from the UPS store to the juice bar is fair game.

pisces.text: Would you care to upgrade, Pisces? With the moon beaming into your sensual (but sensible) second house, you’re willing to splurge on quality. Review your financials: Is there room to indulge? As long as it’s practical and functional, you can consider it an investment. Funds too tight for that go-with-everything fall bag or wellness gadget? Create a special savings account and make your first deposit today. This will motivate you to keep on hustling, even if your gratification is delayed.

items.title: Sleep-Wake Cycle Profiles and Incident Dementia and Cognitive Decline in Older Adults
items.originalTitle: Sleep-Wake Cycle Profiles and Incident Dementia and Cognitive Decline in Older Adults
items.summary: Importance: Sleep-wake cycle (SWC) disruptions are common in patients with dementia and potentially also in the preclinical phase of the disease.
items.caution: A link, not proof of cause.
items.abstract:
Importance: Sleep-wake cycle (SWC) disruptions are common in patients with dementia and potentially also in the preclinical phase of the disease. Accelerometers allow objective measures of multiple SWC dimensions: rest-activity rhythm (RAR), daytime activity, sleep, and chronotype, but these dimensions are rarely examined together.

Objective: This study examined the association of SWC profiles, incorporating the 4 SWC dimensions, with incident dementia and cognitive decline.

Design, setting, and participants: Prospective, UK population-based cohort study based on accelerometer data from the 2012 to 2013 wave of the Whitehall II cohort study, with a median (IQR) follow-up of 12.3 (12.0-12.7) years. Statistical analyses were conducted from June 2025 to March 2026. Participants were dementia-free aged 60 years or older with valid accelerometer data and covariates at baseline.

Exposure: Nine SWC profiles derived from 36 SWC metrics.

Main outcomes and measures: Incident dementia cases until March 2025 were retrieved from electronic health records. Cognitive tests were administered in 2012 to 2013, 2015 to 2016, and 2019 to 2022 and each test score was standardized based on 2012 to 2013 data and all tests averaged to derive a global cognitive z score.

Results: Among 3973 participants (median [IQR] age = 68.4 [64.7 to 74.0] years; 26% women), 379 dementia cases were recorded during a median 12.3-year follow-up. Compared with participants with robust RAR (high level and amplitude, stable, not fragmented), light-intensity physical activity (PA) and good sleep (profile 3), those with poorer RAR (low level and amplitude, unstable, fragmented) along with low PA and poor sleep (profile 7), or with high level and low amplitude RAR and restless sleep (profile 8) had higher dementia risk (hazard ratio, 1.94 [95% CI, 1.32 to 2.84], and 1.96 [95% CI, 1.27 to 3.03], respectively). In analyses on cognitive decline (3806 participants), profile 7 as well as the most sedentary profile with the poorest RAR (profile 9) had faster 10-year cognitive decline (-0.14 [95% CI, -0.26 to -0.02]) and -0.28 [95% CI, -0.44 to -0.13], respectively). Cognitive outcomes in participants with robust RAR and higher PA were similar, irrespective of sleep.

items.title: Medical Imaging and Pediatric and Adolescent Brain Tumor Risk
items.originalTitle: Medical Imaging and Pediatric and Adolescent Brain Tumor Risk
items.summary: Importance: Ionizing radiation from medical imaging may increase brain tumor risk. Objective: To quantify brain tumor risk associated with radiation exposure from medical imaging in children and adolescents.
items.caution: A link, not proof of cause.
items.abstract:
Importance: Ionizing radiation from medical imaging may increase brain tumor risk.

Objective: To quantify brain tumor risk associated with radiation exposure from medical imaging in children and adolescents.

Design, setting, and participants: Retrospective cohort study of children born from 1996 through 2016 who were enrolled from birth in 6 US health care systems or Ontario, Canada, and were alive and cancer-free at age 2 years, with follow-up through December 31, 2017 (US sites), and December 31, 2024 (Ontario).

Exposures: Cumulative radiation dose to the brain from medical imaging, lagged by 2 years.

Main outcomes and measures: Incident brain or other central nervous system tumors. Hazard ratios (HRs) were estimated using Cox proportional hazards models for categorical dose, and excess relative risks (ERRs) were estimated using linear dose-response models for continuous dose.

Results: Among 3 704 860 children (1 900 285 [51.3%] male) followed up for 45 671 641 person-years (mean follow-up, 12.3 years), 1536 brain tumors were diagnosed. Mean radiation dose from 1 head computed tomography (CT) examination was 66.2 mGy (SD, 22.2). Among children with cumulative dose of 1 mGy or greater, mean cumulative dose was 73 mGy (SD, 95) overall and 100 mGy (SD, 105) among those diagnosed with brain tumors. Compared with no exposure, brain tumor risk increased with cumulative dose (>0 to <1 mGy: HR, 1.12 [95% CI, 1.01-1.26]; 1 to <5 mGy: HR, 1.71 [95% CI, 0.88-2.96]; 5 to <50 mGy: HR, 1.86 [95% CI, 1.16-2.81]; 50 to <75 mGy: HR, 2.30 [95% CI, 1.64-3.12]; 75 to <100 mGy: HR, 2.02 [95% CI, 1.13-3.30]; 100 to <150 mGy: HR, 2.81 [95% CI, 1.53-4.66]; ≥150 mGy: HR, 3.85 [95% CI, 2.43-5.75]). Cumulative dose was associated with brain tumor risk overall (ERR per 100 mGy, 1.27 [95% CI, 0.83-1.77]; P < .001), with stronger associations for aggressive histologies (ERR per 100 mGy, 1.51 [95% CI, 1.00-2.11]; P < .001). By age 21 years, exposure comparable to 1 head CT was associated with 7.9 excess brain tumors per 10 000 children, or approximately 1 excess tumor per 1266 head CT examinations. The estimated population-attributable fraction was 10.1% (95% CI, 5.8%-14.2%).

Conclusions and relevance: Medical imaging in children and adolescents was associated with a dose-related increase in brain tumor risk. These findings support careful clinical justification and dose minimization when pediatric imaging using ionizing radiation is indicated.

items.title: Generational gains in cognitive capacity and dementia incidence rates in Western countries
items.originalTitle: Generational gains in cognitive capacity and dementia incidence rates in Western countries
items.summary: The risk of developing dementia at any given age has fallen steadily in Europe and the United States over recent decades.
items.caution: A link, not proof of cause.
items.abstract: The risk of developing dementia at any given age has fallen steadily in Europe and the United States over recent decades. A key unresolved question is whether recent generations reach older age with better cognitive capacity, experience slower cognitive decline, or both, as this has implications for when preventive interventions are likely to have the greatest impact. Analyzing ~783,000 episodic-memory assessments from ~219,000 individuals in five longitudinal studies followed for up to 30 years, we find that later-born generations benefit from a double dividend, with higher memory levels entering old age and slower decline thereafter. The combined advantage is large enough to plausibly account for the reported 13% per-decade decline in dementia incidence. Improvements are concentrated among the fastest decliners; later-born generations show longer periods of stable memory, and their slower decline is mirrored by lower rates of clinical impairment and slower hippocampal atrophy. Calendar-time trends affecting all generations simultaneously are unlikely to explain these differences. Because memory level is built mainly in early life whereas the rate of decline is shaped by conditions in adulthood, sustaining the decline in dementia incidence will require prevention policies that protect brain health across the whole lifespan, beginning in childhood.

items.title: CD49f identifies stem-like memory T cells with enhanced therapeutic potency
items.originalTitle: CD49f identifies stem-like memory T cells with enhanced therapeutic potency
items.summary: The efficacy of adoptive cell therapies depends on the presence of T cells with durable self-renewal, proliferative capacity, and differentiation potential, yet heterogeneity within starting cell populations remains a major barrier to consistent clinical outcomes.
items.caution: A link, not proof of cause.
items.source: Proceedings of the National Academy of Sciences of the United States of America
items.abstract: The efficacy of adoptive cell therapies depends on the presence of T cells with durable self-renewal, proliferative capacity, and differentiation potential, yet heterogeneity within starting cell populations remains a major barrier to consistent clinical outcomes. Here, we identify CD49f as a marker of a unique subset of human memory T cells with stem-like characteristics. CD49fHi memory CD8+ and CD4+ T cells exhibited transcriptional and phenotypic features associated with T cell stemness, including elevated LEF1, TCF1, CCR7, CD27, and CD28, while CD49fLo cells exhibited effector-like transcriptional programs. Clinical evaluation of solid-organ transplant recipients treated with virus-specific T cells for cytomegalovirus complications demonstrated that autologous T cell therapies manufactured from CD49fHi-enriched T cells were associated with superior immune reconstitution and greater in vivo expansion of CMV-specific T cells. Functional assays further revealed that CD49fHi memory T cells possessed enhanced proliferative capacity and transcriptional plasticity following activation. Consistent with these findings, CD19 CAR T cells engineered from CD49fHi memory T cells demonstrated improved persistence and conferred superior survival in a preclinical lymphoma model. Together, these findings establish CD49f as a marker of a stem-like memory T cell subset with enhanced therapeutic potential and identify CD49fHi enrichment as a practical strategy to improve the consistency, durability, and clinical efficacy of both virus-specific and CAR T cell therapies.

items.title: Beyond antigens: TLR9-β-glucan nanocomplexes for 'X' respiratory viral infections
items.originalTitle: Beyond antigens: TLR9-β-glucan nanocomplexes for 'X' respiratory viral infections
items.summary: Pathogen-specific vaccines provide durable immunity, but the delayed rollout during emerging viral outbreaks leaves populations vulnerable. Tobuse et al.
items.caution: A link, not proof of cause.
items.abstract: Pathogen-specific vaccines provide durable immunity, but the delayed rollout during emerging viral outbreaks leaves populations vulnerable. Tobuse et al. address this gap, demonstrating that intranasal administration of K3-SPG, an antigen-free, water-soluble β-glucan/Toll-like receptor 9 (TLR9)-agonist nanocomplex induces biphasic, tissue-restricted innate memory, conferring broad, antigen-independent protection against diverse respiratory viruses by limiting lung pathology.

items.originalTitle: Posterior alpha/beta oscillations reflect oculomotor dynamics underlying subsequent memory effects
items.summary: Neural activity and eye movements are well-established predictors of human memory performance. items.abstract: Neural activity and eye movements are well-established predictors of human memory performance. Successful memory formation is associated with reduced alpha/beta power and increased eye movements. However, their coupling and combined contribution to memory formation remain largely unknown. Across four experiments combining eye tracking with scalp or intracranial electroencephalography during free or constrained viewing, we identify the degree of visual exploration, rather than subsequent memory performance, as consistent modulator of posterior alpha/beta power. Going beyond correlations, manipulating eye movements dissociated alpha/beta power reductions from memory. Together with the finding that saccade parameters predicted alpha/beta dynamics, our results directly link posterior alpha/beta activity to the oculomotor system. Moreover, the accumulation of saccades over time accounted for reduced alpha/beta power, resembling the canonical post-stimulus alpha/beta pattern. Our work demonstrates that posterior alpha/beta activity strongly reflects eye movements, supporting alternative perspectives on alpha/beta subsequent memory effects and the general function of posterior alpha/beta activity.

items.title: Microglia mediate motor memory decay through activity-dependent phagocytosis of myelin sheaths
items.originalTitle: Microglia mediate motor memory decay through activity-dependent phagocytosis of myelin sheaths
items.summary: Experience-dependent changes in myelination are important for motor learning, with newly generated oligodendrocytes contributing to the formation of new myelin. However, motor memories decay over time and the underlying mechanisms remain largely unexplored.
items.caution: In animals or cells — may not carry over to people.
items.abstract: Experience-dependent changes in myelination are important for motor learning, with newly generated oligodendrocytes contributing to the formation of new myelin. However, motor memories decay over time and the underlying mechanisms remain largely unexplored. Here we show that motor memory decay is linked to changes in memory-associated myelin sheaths resulting from microglial phagocytosis in mouse brain. Mechanistically, reduced activity of motor memory engram cells lowers oligodendrocyte expression of the 'don't eat me' signal from Cluster of differentiation 47 (CD47), facilitating microglial phagocytosis and driving myelin loss. Knockout of CD47 from motor memory-associated oligodendrocytes increased microglial phagocytosis of myelin sheaths and accelerated the decay of motor memory, whereas overexpression of CD47 showed opposite results. Moreover, microglia phagocytose myelin sheaths and synapses independently. Our findings reveal that microglial phagocytosis of motor memory-associated myelin sheaths leads to the decay of motor memory. Since various types of memory require myelination in the brain, this mechanism may contribute to the decay of other memory types.

items.title: Genome writing reveals SVA retrotransposon consequences in X-linked dystonia-parkinsonism
items.originalTitle: Genome writing reveals SVA retrotransposon consequences in X-linked dystonia-parkinsonism
items.summary: Human retrotransposon insertions are often associated with diseases. Regarding neurodegenerative X-linked dystonia-parkinsonism (XDP), a human-specific SINE-VNTR-Alu (SVA) subfamily F retrotransposon was inserted in intron 32 of the TAF1 gene.
items.caution: A link, not proof of cause.
items.abstract: Human retrotransposon insertions are often associated with diseases. Regarding neurodegenerative X-linked dystonia-parkinsonism (XDP), a human-specific SINE-VNTR-Alu (SVA) subfamily F retrotransposon was inserted in intron 32 of the TAF1 gene. Here, we genomically rewrote a portion of the mouse Taf1 allele with the corresponding 78-kb XDP patient-derived TAF1 allele. In mouse embryonic stem cells (mESCs), the presence of the intronic SVA-rather than the hybrid gene structure-reduces hyTAF1 (hybrid TAF1 mRNA) levels. This leads to transcriptional downregulation of genes with TATA boxes enriched in their promoters and triggers apoptosis. Chromatin and transcriptome profiling revealed that intronic SVAs are actively transcribed, forming barriers that likely impede transcription elongation. In mice, neuronal-lineage TAF1 humanization resulted in lethality in male progeny within 2 months. XDP male mice developed severe atrophy centered on the striatum-the same brain region affected in XDP patients. Lastly, CRISPRa-mediated activation of hyTAF1 restored mESC viability, suggesting that boosting TAF1 transcription could be a therapeutic approach.

items.title: Multidomain interventions for dementia prevention: a large‑scale systematic review and meta‑analysis of 27 randomized controlled trials
items.originalTitle: Multidomain interventions for dementia prevention: a large‑scale systematic review and meta‑analysis of 27 randomized controlled trials
items.summary: This study aimed to evaluate the effects of multidomain interventions on dementia risk scores and cognitive composite scores and to explore the influence of study, participant, and intervention characteristics on effect estimates.
items.caution: Strongest kind of evidence — still check who took part.
items.source: Alzheimer's & dementia : the journal of the Alzheimer's Association
items.abstract:
Background: This study aimed to evaluate the effects of multidomain interventions on dementia risk scores and cognitive composite scores and to explore the influence of study, participant, and intervention characteristics on effect estimates.

Methods: Five electronic databases (PubMed, Embase, Cochrane Library, CINAHL, and PsycINFO) were systematically searched from inception to March 2026. Randomized controlled trials that assessed multidomain interventions on the outcomes of dementia risk scores and cognitive composite scores were included. The standardized mean difference (SMD) was calculated using random-effects models.

Results: Twenty-seven randomized controlled trials comprising 20,751 participants were included. Multidomain interventions had small but significant effects on both dementia risk scores (SMD = -0.11; p < 0.001) and cognitive composite scores (SMD = 0.12; p < 0.001). Interventions combining physical activity, nutrition, cognitive training, and social engagement were associated with greater reductions in dementia risk scores (subgroup difference p = 0.018).

Discussion: Multidomain interventions have a small but significant effect, reducing dementia risk scores and improving composite cognitive scores.
